title: Review: Lipids: triglycerides; Phospholipids, steroids and other lipids; Nucleotides, DNA and RNA structure; Amino acids and peptide bonds
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM10a#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM10a#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM10a#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM06#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM05#N.14, BM06#N.6b, BM07#N.2b, BM10a#N.9, BM10b#N.15, BM05#N.9b, BM06#N.9b, BM07#N.6b, BM10a#N.8, BM06#N.14, BM07#N.4b, BM10a#N.2b. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Deoxyribose
items.clue: The 5-carbon sugar found in the monomers of DNA

items.label: Uracil
items.clue: Base found in RNA in place of T; it pairs with A

items.label: Nucleotide
items.clue: Monomer of DNA and RNA: a pentose, a phosphate and a base

items.label: Hydrophilic
items.clue: Describes the charged phosphate head, which interacts with water

questions.stem: To make a spread, manufacturers react a liquid vegetable oil with hydrogen, using a catalyst. Some C=C double bonds in its fatty acid chains become C–C single bonds. How does the oil change?

options.text: It becomes more liquid, as double bonds stiffen chains and hold molecules together.
It becomes more unsaturated, as it now carries more hydrogen atoms.
It becomes more solid, as straighter chains pack more closely together.
It becomes more solid, as the extra bonds need more heat to break when it melts.

questions.explanation: Fewer kinks, closer packing, stronger attractions between molecules: a higher melting point. A liquid oil becomes a soft solid, like butter in the hook.

questions.stem: In a plasma membrane, the phosphate heads of the phospholipids face the cytosol and the extracellular fluid, and the fatty acid tails face each other in the interior of the membrane. Which statement best explains this arrangement?

options.text: The tails are the polar part of each molecule, and polar groups strongly attract one another.
The cell places each phospholipid so that its tail is shielded from the surrounding water.
The heads are polar and interact with water, while the nonpolar tails are kept away from it.
The heads are too large to fit inside the membrane, so the thin tails pack there instead.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the R groups of amino acids?

options.text: They are the same in every amino acid, which differ instead in their amine and carboxyl groups.
They form the covalent bonds that join each amino acid to the next one in the chain.
They are nitrogenous bases that pair with one another to hold the chain in its shape.
They differ among amino acids, and their chemical properties affect how the chain folds.

questions.explanation: The R group is the only part that differs. Whether it is nonpolar, polar or ionic decides which interactions it forms, and so how that region of the protein folds.

questions.stem: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA from a hypothetical bacterium shows that 21% of its nitrogenous bases are adenine. What percentage of its bases are cytosine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so T = A = 21% and A + T = 42%. That leaves 100% − 42% = 58% for C and G together, and because C = G, cytosine is 58%/2 = 29%.

questions.stem: Two DNA molecules from two hypothetical species of bacteria each contain the same number of nucleotides, and in both, 30% of the bases are adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine. The two molecules carry different genetic information. Which statement best explains how this is possible?

options.text: The amino acids attached along their strands are arranged in a different order in each.
The nucleotides of each species are built around a different five-carbon sugar.
Each molecule is folded into a different three-dimensional shape that stores information.
Their nucleotides are arranged in a different order along each molecule.

questions.stem: Seals that live in polar seas have a thick layer of fat, called blubber, beneath the skin. A seal's body is kept at about 37 °C, while the surrounding water is near 0 °C. Which statement best describes how the blubber helps keep the seal's body warm?

options.text: It reduces how quickly the seal's body loses heat to the sea around it.
Its fat is turned into heat at the same rate as heat escapes from the body.
It keeps the cold of the water from moving in and cooling the seal's body.
It stops heat from leaving the body at all, so the seal loses no heat to the sea.

questions.explanation: Fat conducts heat poorly, so blubber reduces the rate at which heat passes from the warm body to the cold water. Metabolism keeps up with the slower loss.

questions.stem: A drug removes most of the cholesterol from the plasma membranes of cultured animal cells but does not otherwise damage the cells. Which prediction about the treated cells is most likely correct?

options.text: They would work better, as cholesterol is harmful to the cells.
They would run short of fuel, as cholesterol is stored for energy.
Their membranes would be less stable, as cholesterol supports their structure.
Their membranes would be unchanged, as the phospholipids are bonded together.

questions.explanation: Cholesterol provides essential structural stability to animal cell membranes. With most of it removed, the membranes would be less stable, more easily damaged and more likely to leak.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by dehydration synthesis. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
298 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule. A chain of 150 needs 149 bonds: 149 water molecules.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how the two strands of a DNA double helix are held together?

options.text: By hydrogen bonds between identical bases, such as A with A, one on each strand
By covalent bonds between complementary bases, with one base on each strand
By hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one base on each strand
By covalent bonds joining the sugar–phosphate backbones of the two strands

questions.explanation: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one from each strand: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. The nucleotides within each strand are joined by covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triglycerides in blood plasma, which is mostly water. Each lipoprotein has an oily core of cholesterol and triglyceride, surrounded by a single layer of phospholipids (with some proteins). How are the phospholipids in this layer most likely arranged?

options.text: Tails facing outwards into the plasma; heads facing inwards into the oily core.
Heads facing outwards into the plasma; tails pointing inwards into the oily core.
Tails joined to one another by covalent bonds, forming a rigid shell around the core.
Mixed evenly through the oily core, as phospholipids are entirely hydrophobic like cholesterol.

questions.stem: During protein synthesis, a free amino acid is joined to the end of a growing polypeptide. Which statement correctly describes how the amino acid becomes part of the polypeptide?

options.text: A water molecule is added between it and the end of the chain, joining the two together.
The chain's last carboxyl group forms a covalent bond with the amino acid's amine group, releasing water.
Its R group forms a covalent bond with the R group of the amino acid at the end of the chain.
Its amine group is held to the carboxyl group at the end of the chain by a hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Each nucleotide in a nucleic acid contains a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. What is its third structural component?

options.text: A five-carbon sugar, ribose in RNA or deoxyribose in DNA
An amino acid, the same monomer that builds a protein
Glucose, a sugar whose molecules contain six carbons
A second base, paired with the first by hydrogen bonds

questions.explanation: Each nucleotide has three components: a five-carbon sugar (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA), a phosphate group and one nitrogenous base.
